reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Defined by an abrupt onset of persistent daily headache that becomes unremitting within a day, in a patient who can often name the exact date it began
The headache is continuous from close to its onset, unlike chronic migraine which evolves from episodic attacks
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, and secondary causes with a similar abrupt daily pattern must be sought
The phenotype may resemble migraine or tension-type headache, which does not exclude the diagnosis
A preceding infection, stressful life event or minor procedure is sometimes reported around the time of onset
Important secondary mimics include low- and high-cerebrospinal-fluid-pressure headaches, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and, in older patients, giant cell arteritis
It is often refractory to treatment, which is generally guided by the predominant migrainous or tension-type phenotype
reference.pathophysiology: The mechanism of new daily persistent headache is unclear. Proposed contributors include a post-infectious or post-inflammatory state with persistent cytokine activation, cervical or ligamentous factors, and disordered central pain processing. Because the abrupt, unremitting pattern can also be produced by disorders of cerebrospinal fluid pressure or venous drainage, these secondary processes must be excluded before the primary label is applied.
additionalDifferentials: Giant cell arteritis in older patients
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain with contrast, looking for pachymeningeal enhancement or other secondary signs
MR or CT venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Consideration of lumbar puncture with opening pressure when a cerebrospinal-fluid-pressure disorder is suspected
Inflammatory markers such as ESR and CRP in older patients to screen for giant cell arteritis
Review of headache-onset timing, triggers and medication use
redFlags: A postural component suggesting a cerebrospinal-fluid-pressure disorder
Papilloedema, visual symptoms or pulsatile tinnitus
Focal neurological deficit, seizures or a thunderclap onset
Age over fifty with scalp tenderness or jaw claudication
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable: some patients remit spontaneously over months, while a persisting subgroup proves refractory to preventive treatment; the prognosis is better when a treatable secondary cause is identified.
pitfalls: Accepting the diagnosis without excluding cerebrospinal-fluid-pressure disorders or venous thrombosis
Overlooking giant cell arteritis in an older patient
Allowing medication-overuse headache to develop during treatment
Assuming a migrainous phenotype rules out a secondary cause
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3)
